Treat the story as a motivating measurement problem; the buoyancy and density reasoning does not depend on every historical detail of the legend being verified.

openstax:12.invitation: Blood slows as it enters many tiny parallel vessels, even though each vessel is narrow. Water near a riverbank can move more slowly than water in the middle. Fluid motion depends on the whole flow path, including branching, pressure changes, and resistance between neighboring layers.

12.1.restored: The aorta-to-capillaries worked example and total area across parallel branches.
12.1.opening: The source compares flow in the aorta with flow through many capillaries. Looking at one narrow capillary alone can lead to the wrong prediction. For the combined branching network, add the cross-sectional areas of all the parallel paths carrying the flow. A much larger total area allows a smaller average speed for the same volume per second. Continuity applies to the whole collection you have chosen, not to an imaginary single tube.

12.4.restored: The riverbank comparison as motivation for velocity gradients and viscosity.
12.4.opening: Imagine watching floating leaves near a riverbank and nearer the middle. Their speeds may differ because the moving water interacts with the boundaries and with neighboring layers. OpenStax uses this observation to introduce flow resistance. The average speed in Q = Av summarizes the whole cross-section; it does not say that every layer moves at that speed. A velocity profile contains information the average hides.

openstax:13.invitation: A thermometer reports a thermal state, a gas pushes on every wall, and cooling humid air can produce droplets. Connect the macroscopic measurements to particles, but keep track of where an idealized particle model stops describing the actual material.

13.4.restored: The gas-volume extrapolation toward absolute zero and the failure of an ideal model at phase changes.
13.4.opening: An ideal-gas volume–temperature graph at fixed pressure suggests a straight line that would reach zero volume at zero kelvin. The source explicitly contrasts that extrapolation with a real gas, which can condense and later solidify. The actual sample does not shrink away to nothing. A straight line within one range of conditions is evidence for a model there, not permission to extend that model through every phase change.

13.6.restored: The familiar humidity observation connected to partial pressure, evaporation, and dew point.
13.6.opening: Why can the same air temperature feel different on dry and humid days? OpenStax connects the question to evaporation: water leaving a surface carries energy, and the surrounding water-vapor partial pressure affects the net rate. Now cool that air without removing vapor. Its relative humidity can rise until condensation becomes favorable. The two observations connect through temperature-dependent saturation, not through a literal container in which air has become 'full of water.'

openstax:14.invitation: A vehicle's brakes warm during a descent, a picnic cooler slows energy transfer, and stored solar energy can warm a building after sunlight fades. Follow the energy through the actual materials and processes: a temperature change is one possible result, but not the only one.

14.2.restored: The source's brake-heating example and explicit energy partition before Q = mcΔT.
14.2.opening: A vehicle descending a hill loses gravitational potential energy. In the source's braking example, only a specified fraction ends up retained as internal energy in the brake material. First determine that energy share, then divide by the brake mass and specific heat to estimate the temperature rise. Applying Q = mcΔT before deciding what Q belongs to would quietly assign all the vehicle's lost energy to one component.

14.7.restored: Mária Telkes and Eleanor Raymond's solar-heated house, including thermal storage.
14.7.opening: OpenStax describes Mária Telkes working with architect Eleanor Raymond on a solar-heated house. Sun-warmed air transferred energy to a storage material so it could be used later. This example joins several ideas: radiation brings in solar energy, moving air transports it, and a material stores it. Designing the system requires more than identifying a sunny surface; the timing of collection and release matters too.

openstax:15.invitation: A toy bird keeps dipping its beak, while a handful of tossed coins usually lands in a mixed arrangement. What supplies the bird's energy, and what makes some large-scale outcomes more likely than others? These questions connect heat engines to the microscopic explanation of entropy.

15.4.restored: The drinking-bird example, with an explicit energy supply and correction of the source caption's perpetual-motion implication.
15.4.opening: The drinking bird pictured in the source seems to keep working for free. Water evaporating from its wet head cools it relative to its surroundings. That temperature difference drives changes in the sealed fluid, shifting the bird's balance so it tips and returns. Follow the energy across the boundary: the surroundings and continuing evaporation sustain the process. This is a real heat-engine demonstration, not a perpetual-motion machine or an exactly reversible Carnot engine.

15.7.restored: The five-coin microstate table and its equal-probability assumption.
15.7.opening: Toss five fair, independent coins. There is only one way to get five heads, but ten distinct arrangements give three heads and two tails. Each particular arrangement has the same probability; the mixed outcome wins because more arrangements count toward it. OpenStax builds the statistical argument from this small, countable example. For a physical system, the next step is to identify the accessible microscopic arrangements and justify the probabilities, rather than treating 'disorder' as a substitute for counting.

openstax:16.invitation: A pendulum can measure gravity, and the shadow of a steadily rotating ball can trace a back-and-forth motion. Use these concrete connections to see what the equations describe before following the same patterns into waves and resonance.

16.4.restored: The pendulum as an instrument for measuring g, including small-angle and precision limits.
16.4.opening: Reverse the usual pendulum question. Instead of using gravity to predict a period, measure the length and period to estimate g = 4π²L/T². The source connects such measurements to geological exploration, where small variations in gravity carry information. A longer timing interval containing several swings helps estimate the period, but precision also depends on measuring the pivot-to-bob distance and keeping the swing small enough for the simple-pendulum approximation.

16.6.restored: The rotating turntable and projected shadow used to construct harmonic motion.
16.6.opening: Imagine a ball fastened near the rim of a vertical turntable. As the turntable rotates steadily, its shadow on a horizontal line moves back and forth. The ball keeps a constant speed around the circle, but the shadow slows near each end and moves fastest through the middle. That projection is the source's bridge to sinusoidal motion: uniform change of angle produces nonuniform change of position along one axis.

openstax:17.invitation: A rustling leaf and a crowded street occupy very different parts of the sound-intensity range. A wind instrument changes pitch as it warms, even if its length stays nearly fixed. Explore what sound carries, how resonant air responds, and what a listener actually detects.

17.3.restored: The quiet-forest and noisy-street comparison motivating a logarithmic intensity scale.
17.3.opening: The source places the faint rustle of leaves beside the sound of a busy street. A useful scale must handle an enormous range of intensities without becoming a list of unwieldy numbers. Decibels compress that range by reporting a logarithm of an intensity ratio. Increasing an intensity level by 10 dB means ten times the physical intensity; it does not mean adding ten units of intensity or guaranteeing that every listener judges the sound ten times as loud.

17.5.restored: Temperature-dependent instrument tuning and the source's closed-tube calculation setup.
17.5.opening: Why do wind players let instruments approach room temperature before tuning together? The source connects pitch to the speed of sound in the air column. For an ideal tube closed at one end, the fundamental satisfies f = v/(4L). Before using a target frequency to calculate a tube length, determine the sound speed at the stated temperature. The geometry sets the allowed wavelength; the air's properties help set the frequency.

openstax:18.invitation: A copier turns a pattern of light into a pattern of powder, and a torsion balance makes a tiny electric interaction measurable. Follow how observations and devices reveal electric forces, including the movement of charge within materials.

18.4.restored: Coulomb's torsion-balance measurement as the experimental basis of the force law.
18.4.opening: An inverse-square law is a claim about measurements, not just a familiar-looking formula. Coulomb used a torsion balance: an electric force twisted a suspended system, and the twist provided a way to measure the force. Changing separation while controlling the charges tested how that force varied with distance. Think of the equation as a compact account of an experiment whose small forces required a sensitive instrument.

18.8.restored: The sequence of xerography, including the photoconductor and the separate fixing stage.
18.8.opening: A copier must turn an optical image into something that can attract toner. In the source's simplified xerographic process, a charged photoconducting surface becomes conducting where light reaches it, changing the charge pattern. Charged toner then collects selectively and transfers to paper. Heated rollers fix the image afterward. Electrostatic attraction explains the temporary placement of the powder; it does not by itself explain why the finished print stays attached.

openstax:19.invitation: A small particle can gain a large speed by crossing a voltage difference. An insulating sheet can change how much charge a capacitor stores. Use energy and the response of materials to connect voltage measurements with what charges actually do.

19.1.restored: The accelerating-electron example and why the electron-volt is useful.
19.1.opening: Imagine accelerating an electron from rest through a potential difference whose magnitude is 50 V. If the electric force supplies the kinetic-energy gain, that gain is 50 eV. A doubly charged ion crossing the same accelerating voltage gains 100 eV. The source uses examples like these to make the electron-volt useful: voltage gives energy per charge, so both the charge and the voltage matter. To calculate speed, bring in the particle's mass as a separate piece of information.

19.5.restored: The microscopic polarization explanation behind a dielectric's macroscopic effect.
19.5.opening: Slide an insulating material between capacitor plates and its charges can respond even though they cannot travel freely across the gap. Bound positive and negative charge shifts slightly, and existing molecular dipoles may reorient. The source's microscopic picture explains how the resulting polarization changes the field. Before predicting a voltage or stored-energy change, ask whether the capacitor remains attached to a battery or has been disconnected: those arrangements hold different quantities fixed.

openstax:20.invitation: A circuit begins responding long before one electron could drift all the way around it. Two lamps can provide similar light while drawing different power. Keep charge transport, energy transfer, and the useful output of a device distinct as you follow a working circuit.

20.1.restored: The filled-straw current analogy and its distinction between carrier motion and response.
20.1.opening: OpenStax suggests a straw containing a row of small objects as an analogy for current: pushing at one end can make something emerge at the other before the original object travels the straw's length. A metal wire likewise already contains mobile charges throughout it. The analogy helps separate a carrier's slow average drift from a circuit's much faster electromagnetic response. It is not an exact model of how the field and energy propagate through a real circuit.

20.4.restored: The lamp energy-cost comparison, retaining the calculation but identifying historical example assumptions.
20.4.opening: The source compares a 60 W lamp with a 15 W lamp chosen to provide similar light output. Over 1,000 hours, they use 60 kWh and 15 kWh, respectively. That calculation separates useful illumination from electrical input: equal brightness need not mean equal power. If comparing total cost, include purchase price, operating time, and replacement life as well as energy. The book's example prices and technology comparisons are assumptions of that example, not current shopping advice.

openstax:21.invitation: Why can a car's lights dim when its starter draws a large current? How can a flash photograph reveal a motion too quick to see? Real sources and time-dependent circuits add behavior that a simple diagram of ideal wires and resistors leaves out.

21.2.restored: Dimming car lights as evidence of load-dependent terminal voltage.
21.2.opening: The source begins with lights connected to a car battery. Adding a heavy load can dim them even when the connecting wires have little resistance. A battery is not a perfectly fixed voltage boundary: current through its internal resistance reduces the voltage available at the terminals. The observation gives the model a job to do. Compare the open-circuit reading with the reading under load, and explain why those two measurements need not agree.

21.6.restored: Harold Edgerton's flash photography and the distinction between stored energy and pulse duration.
21.6.opening: Harold 'Doc' Edgerton's photographs made fast events visible, including a splashing drop of milk. The source uses a strobe-light problem to connect that achievement to a capacitor. The stored energy must be sufficient for the flash, while the discharge must be short enough that the subject barely moves during it. Those are two requirements: the capacitor's energy and the circuit's time scale answer different design questions.

openstax:22.invitation: A wire's current direction does not by itself reveal the sign of its moving charges. A magnetic measurement can help. Follow this experimental thread from the Hall effect to instruments that separate particles by their mass-to-charge ratio.

22.6.restored: Hall-voltage polarity as evidence about charge carriers, with the simple-carrier-model qualification.
22.6.opening: Two strips can carry conventional current in the same direction while having different kinds of mobile charge. In the source's simple model, positive carriers and negative carriers moving in opposite directions are pushed toward the same side by a fixed magnetic field, but they leave opposite signs of charge there. The transverse voltage therefore reverses sign. With current and field directions known, this provides evidence about the carriers; interpreting more complicated materials can require more than this one-carrier model.

22.11.restored: Mass spectrometry as an identification problem and the need to control velocity and charge state.
22.11.opening: A laboratory may need to distinguish ions that look identical to the eye. The source's mass spectrometer first selects a speed, then bends the transmitted beam in a magnetic field. A detector records where the ions arrive. Interpreting the separation requires knowing what was controlled: different radii reveal different mass-to-charge ratios at the selected speed, not mass alone when charge states differ. The apparatus turns invisible particle properties into measurable positions.

openstax:23.invitation: A meter responds when a nearby circuit switches on—and again, in the opposite direction, when it switches off. A solid metal plate can be slowed by a magnet without touching it. Start with these observations and track the changing flux and the energy transfer they reveal.

23.1.restored: Faraday's two-circuit switching experiment and the contrast between steady field and changing flux.
23.1.opening: Place two coils near one another, with a battery and switch connected to one and a sensitive meter connected to the other. The source describes a deflection when the switch closes and an opposite deflection when it opens. Holding the switch closed does not maintain that induced current once conditions settle. This sequence is the clue: the second circuit responds to changing magnetic flux, not simply to the continued presence of a magnetic field.

23.4.restored: Magnetic damping, cut slots, and the contrasting uses of eddy-current energy transfer.
23.4.opening: A solid conducting plate swinging into a magnetic-field region can slow sharply, even without a wire wound into a visible coil. Current loops form inside the metal. Cutting slots into the plate interrupts many of those paths and changes the damping. The same energy account connects two applications in the source: magnetic braking removes mechanical energy, while induction heating deliberately transfers electrical energy into the material's internal energy.

openstax:24.invitation: Electricity, magnetism, and light once seemed like separate subjects. Maxwell's theory connected them, and instruments now reveal parts of the electromagnetic spectrum our eyes cannot see. Ask what a different wavelength lets an observer learn, not just what that wavelength is called.

24.1.restored: Maxwell's synthesis and the predictive connection between changing fields and light.
24.1.opening: Maxwell brought together results from experimenters and theorists including Coulomb, Oersted, Gauss, and Faraday. A crucial addition connected changing electric fields to magnetic fields. The combined theory supported traveling electromagnetic disturbances with a predicted vacuum speed matching the measured speed of light. The achievement was more than collecting formulas: a theory of electric and magnetic phenomena explained something already familiar from a different part of physics.

24.3.restored: George Carruthers's Apollo 16 ultraviolet instrument and its view of Earth's atmosphere.
24.3.opening: During Apollo 16, an ultraviolet camera and spectrograph designed by George Carruthers observed from the Moon. One striking subject was Earth itself: ultraviolet images revealed atmospheric emission and structure that a visible-light photograph would not show in the same way. The source uses this instrument to make the spectrum concrete. Choosing a wavelength range changes which physical processes stand out, while the detector translates otherwise invisible radiation into an image we can examine.

openstax:25.invitation: A fish can appear displaced—or even appear in two places when viewed through a tank corner. A rainbow can be investigated using a large water-filled vessel. Trace the light that reaches an observer and connect each change of direction to a particular boundary.

25.3.restored: The fish-tank corner and multiple refracted paths to the observer.
25.3.opening: Looking through the corner of a fish tank can produce two apparent images of one fish. Light from the fish reaches the observer along different paths through the tank's faces. The eye extends each arriving direction backward as though the path had stayed straight, placing the apparent fish in different locations. The animal has not moved or multiplied; the path of the information reaching the observer has changed.

25.5.restored: Al-Farisi's large water-drop model and the experimental history of rainbow explanations.
25.5.opening: How could someone study the path of light inside a tiny raindrop? The source describes Kamal al-Din al-Farisi using a water-filled glass vessel as a large model, with controlled illumination in a darkened chamber. Theodoric of Freiberg pursued related experiments, building on earlier optical work. Enlarging the system made its behavior easier to investigate. Follow both refraction and internal reflection in the model, then ask how their combined effect depends on wavelength.

openstax:26.invitation: A microscope and a telescope both use an image made by one optical element as the object for another. Yet they solve different viewing problems. Follow the image through the instrument, paying attention to angular size, focus, and the limits of the simple lens model.

26.4.restored: Parfocal microscope objectives and image-by-image reasoning through an instrument.
26.4.opening: Look at a microscope's rotating set of objectives. The source notes that objectives can be arranged to be parfocal, so changing magnification leaves the specimen close to focus. Inside the optical path, the objective's image becomes the eyepiece's object. Analyze those stages in order: the second lens receives light from an already formed image, not directly from the specimen as though the first lens were absent.

26.5.restored: The source's comparison of Galilean and two-converging-lens telescopes.
26.5.opening: Galileo's telescope used a converging objective and a diverging eyepiece, producing an upright view. The source contrasts it with a simple telescope using two converging lenses. Both can enlarge the angle a distant object subtends at the eye, but they do not produce the same intermediate ray geometry or image orientation. A sketch of the rays tells you more than the statement that a telescope contains two lenses.

openstax:27.invitation: A soap film changes color as it thins, while a transparent specimen can remain hard to see even when it is magnified. Light's wave behavior explains both the limits of an image and techniques that make hidden detail visible.

27.7.restored: Agnes Pockels's surface-film investigations and the changing color of a film.
27.7.opening: Watch the bands of color move across a draining soap film. The material need not acquire new pigments as it thins; the changing thickness changes how reflected light interferes. The source connects surface-film investigations to Agnes Pockels, who built a trough from homemade materials and carried out experiments despite barriers to formal scientific participation. A familiar kitchen material can become a carefully controlled physical system.

27.9.restored: The distinction between resolution and contrast in microscopy.
27.9.opening: Suppose a microscope has enough resolving power to distinguish a specimen's structure, but almost all the illumination passes through it. The image may still be difficult to interpret because neighboring regions have nearly equal brightness. The source separates this contrast problem from the wavelength limit on resolution. A specimen can alter phase without absorbing much light; suitable interference methods turn that otherwise hard-to-see difference into a brightness difference.

openstax:28.invitation: Two observers can agree about which flashes arrive at one person's eyes first while disagreeing about whether the distant lamps emitted simultaneously. Even charging a battery changes the energy—and therefore the rest mass—of a system. Examine the measurement procedure before deciding what relativity predicts.

28.2.restored: The train-and-lamps thought experiment with arrival events separated from emission times.
28.2.opening: In the source's train experiment, lamps flash at opposite ends and an observer rides between them. A second observer describes that rider moving toward one arriving flash and away from the other. Both observers agree on the order in which light reaches the rider; those arrivals occur at the rider's location. The disagreement concerns the time coordinates assigned to the separated emission events after accounting for propagation. Keep these two pairs of events distinct as you reason through simultaneity.

28.6.restored: The charged-battery mass example as an everyday application of system rest energy.
28.6.opening: The source asks whether charging a battery increases its rest mass. In the idealized energy account, retaining an additional energy ΔE increases the complete battery's rest mass by ΔE/c². The increase is tiny because c² is enormous. Nothing needs to travel near light speed for this relation to matter in principle: stored chemical energy contributes to the mass of the resting system. Use the net energy retained, not energy lost as heat elsewhere during charging.

openstax:29.invitation: A glowing gas produces separated spectral lines rather than every possible color. Electrons can diffract, yet a rolling bowling ball does not display a visible interference pattern. Let these observations set the questions that quantization and matter waves must answer.

29.1.restored: Emission spectra as useful experimental fingerprints before their quantum explanation.
29.1.opening: Pass an electrical discharge through a gas and examine its light with a spectroscope. The source's oxygen spectrum contains separated lines, a pattern that can identify the substance. Scientists could use such patterns before they understood why only certain energies appeared. Quantization addresses that missing explanation: allowed changes in atomic or molecular energy produce specific photon energies. An empirical fingerprint and a theory explaining it are different achievements.

29.6.restored: De Broglie's proposal and the numerical bowling-ball wavelength comparison.
29.6.opening: De Broglie's proposal raises an immediate objection: if matter has a wavelength, why does a bowling ball look so ordinary? Use the source's 3 kg ball moving at 10 m/s. Its momentum is 30 kg·m/s, so λ = h/p is about 2.2 × 10⁻³⁵ m. The wavelength is extraordinarily small compared with the openings and obstacles in the bowling alley. This scale comparison explains why a successful quantum relation need not produce a visible wave pattern in an everyday setting.

openstax:30.invitation: A few alpha particles scattered backward through a thin foil forced a major revision of atomic structure. A scorpion glowing under ultraviolet illumination reveals another kind of atomic and molecular evidence. Connect each observation to what it tells us—and what the model still has to explain.

30.2.restored: The surprising rare large-angle scattering events and their power to discriminate atomic models.
30.2.opening: Most alpha particles passed through a thin gold foil with little deflection. That was unsurprising. The source emphasizes the small fraction scattered through very large angles, some almost straight back. A diffuse distribution of positive charge could not readily account for those events. The rare observations mattered disproportionately: they pointed toward a compact, massive, positively charged nucleus. A good model must explain the unusual part of a distribution as well as its most common result.

30.5.restored: The fluorescent scorpion and the distinction between absorbed and emitted photon energy.
30.5.opening: The source shows a scorpion glowing visibly under ultraviolet illumination. The visible photons are not simply reflected ultraviolet photons; the material absorbs energy and later emits at different energies. Molecular and atomic energy changes, including nonradiative transfers, complete the account. Fluorescence makes an invisible part of the illumination visible while reminding us to track all the energy, not require each outgoing photon to match an incoming photon's energy.

openstax:31.invitation: An invisible interaction can become a flash of light and then an electrical pulse. An alpha particle can escape a nucleus even when a classical energy diagram appears to trap it. Follow the evidence from the detector back to the physical model.

31.2.restored: The scintillator–photomultiplier detection chain and the relation between event and signal.
31.2.opening: A scintillation detector makes a chain of translations. Incoming radiation transfers energy to a material; the material emits a small light flash; a photosensitive device converts that light into an electrical signal. In the source's photomultiplier example, successive stages amplify the signal into something measurable. A recorded pulse is therefore evidence of an interaction processed by an instrument. Its size and timing depend on both the radiation and the detector's response.

31.7.restored: The alpha-decay barrier puzzle, without the source's misleading claim that the particle skips the intervening region.
31.7.opening: Draw the potential-energy barrier surrounding a nucleus, then mark the measured energy of an emitted alpha particle below the barrier's top. Classically, it could not climb out with that energy. The source introduces Gamow's tunneling explanation to resolve the puzzle. The quantum wavefunction extends through the barrier and into the outside region with a small transmitted amplitude. No extra energy has to be borrowed to carry the particle over the top, and the explanation does not require the wavefunction to vanish in the intervening region.

openstax:32.invitation: A detector must learn where radiation came from, not merely that some arrived. A nuclear-energy calculation must distinguish the energy available from the rate at which a device delivers it. Those measurement and accounting questions run through this chapter's imaging and energy applications.

32.1.restored: The gamma camera's collimator, signal chain, and missing depth information.
32.1.opening: The source's gamma-camera diagram puts a collimator in front of the detectors. Its openings select incoming directions, helping the system associate a detected signal with a location in the projected image. Scintillators and photosensors then turn the radiation interaction into an electrical record. In this simple arrangement, different depths along the same viewing direction can contribute to the same image location. Forming a two-dimensional projection is not the same measurement as reconstructing a three-dimensional distribution.

32.5.restored: The fusion-fuel worked example's conversion from energy per reaction to total energy and average power.
32.5.opening: The source works from energy released in one fusion reaction to the energy available from a stated mass of reactants. That requires counting reactions, with the correct mixture of nuclei. It then spreads the total energy over a year to find an average power and considers a separate conversion efficiency for electricity. A large energy per kilogram is only the beginning of an engineering account: it does not specify the reaction rate, operating losses, or net electrical output.

openstax:33.invitation: A theory can suggest a particle before an experiment produces evidence for it. An accelerator can build a large particle energy through many modest steps. Follow how a proposed interaction becomes a testable prediction and how an apparatus creates the conditions needed to test it.

33.1.restored: Yukawa's predicted mass scale followed by cosmic-ray evidence and laboratory production of pions.
33.1.opening: Yukawa's proposal linked a short interaction range to a massive exchanged particle at a time when no suitable particle had been identified. The source then follows the experimental story: pions were observed in cosmic-ray experiments in 1947 and later produced in accelerators. The narrative distinguishes a virtual exchange in an interaction model from a real particle that can be created and detected when a collision supplies sufficient energy and momentum.
